Kassa
kah'shah
n. (city of Upper Hungary, Slovak Kosice; where the diets of Bocskai and Bethlen confirmed Protestant liberties)
From Hungarian Kassa, of uncertain origin; Slovak Kosice, German Kaschau.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kassa was the chief city of Upper Hungary and the place where Hungarian Protestantism won its legal standing. Stephen Bocskai made it his seat during the rising of 1604 to 1606 that produced the Peace of Vienna, the first imperial guarantee of Protestant worship in Hungary; Gabriel Bethlen held diets there; and the city's cathedral passed back and forth between the confessions as the balance shifted. Those liberties were real, repeatedly confirmed, and repeatedly narrowed, and the Hungarian Protestants spent the seventeenth century defending a charter rather than simply preaching. The dictionary records Kassa because legal liberty is a genuine mercy and a standing temptation: a church that has secured its freedom must still be asked what it is doing with it. “ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh” (Gal 5:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines liberty as freedom from restraint and the power of acting as one thinks fit, free as being at liberty and not under restraint, and toleration as the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.

expand to see more

LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit.

FREE, a. Being at liberty; not being under necessity or restraint, physical or moral.

TOLERATION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.

SERVANT, n. A person, male or female, that attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him.

Key Scripture

1Pe 2:16 — "As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God."

Jam 1:25 — "But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed."

Modern Corruption

Bocskai's seat and Bethlen's diets, where Hungarian Protestant worship was first guaranteed by imperial peace.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern reading of Christian liberty as the right to do as one pleases in matters God has not expressly forbidden, which is precisely the construction Paul forecloses. The Hungarian churches won a liberty of worship; the question Scripture puts to them and to us is what the liberty is for.

The principle to recover is that liberty is freedom to serve and never a licence for the flesh. Paul states the calling and the limit in one sentence: “ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13). Peter puts the two together as a paradox that is not one: “As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God” (1Pe 2:16). James calls the law itself the law of liberty and makes doing the test: “whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed” (Jam 1:25). And lawful is not the same as wise: “All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient” (1Co 10:23).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eleutheria (G1657), liberty; Greek douleuo (G1398), to serve as a bondman.

Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty, freedom from bondage; Galatians 5:13.

Greek aphorme (G874) — an occasion, a base of operations; Galatians 5:13.

Greek epikalumma (G1942) — a covering, a cloke for evil; 1 Peter 2:16.

Greek parakupto (G3879) — to stoop and look into; James 1:25.

Greek sumphero (G4851) — to be profitable, expedient; 1 Corinthians 10:23.

Usage

"“use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh” (Gal 5:13) — Bocskai's rising, 1604 to 1606."

"“not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness” (1Pe 2:16) — the Peace of Vienna and Bethlen's diets."

"“All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient” (1Co 10:23) — a cathedral passing between confessions."
